hints: Think about what provides enough energy in nature to break the very strong $N\equiv N$ bond in air without human help.
Think about where very high temperatures occur in everyday transport that allow $N_2$ and $O_2$ from air to react together.
walkthrough:
Why $N_2$ needs extreme energy to react**
Nitrogen gas is very unreactive because of its strong triple bond. Only a huge burst of energy will split $N_2$ so it can combine with $O_2$ to make $NO_x$. In nature that burst comes from the sky.

Match natural and man-made high temperature sources**
Lightning heats air to thousands of degrees and forms $NO$ naturally. In a car engine the spark and hot combustion does the same thing to air drawn into the cylinder, so exhaust gases contain $NO_x$ as the man-made source.

Final answer: natural: lightning
man-made: internal combustion engines / car engines

hints: Remember $NO_2$ dissolves in rain water to give a mixture of nitrous acid and nitric acid, or nitric acid alone if oxygen is also present.
walkthrough:
Form acids directly from $NO_2$**
When $NO_2$ meets water droplets it disproportionates. One $N$ is reduced and one is oxidised, giving $HNO_2$ and $HNO_3$ together: $$2NO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow HNO_2 + HNO_3$$ This acidic solution falls as acid rain.

hints: Recall photochemical smog needs sunlight, $NO_2$ and another type of pollutant from unburned fuel.
walkthrough:
Link $NO_2$ to smog ingredients**
Photochemical smog forms on sunny days when $NO_2$ and unburned hydrocarbons, also called volatile organic compounds (VOCs), from petrol vapour and exhaust mix in sunlight. Their reaction builds up peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN.
Final answer: $NO_2$ reacts with unburned hydrocarbons / VOCs to form PAN.

hints: Treat this as a normal acid plus basic oxide reaction giving a salt plus water, then balance Ca and nitrate.
walkthrough:
Write the neutralisation**
Nitric acid neutralises the basic oxide $CaO$. Calcium needs two nitrate ions to balance $Ca^{2+}$, so two $HNO_3$ are needed: $$2HNO_3 + CaO \rightarrow Ca(NO_3)_2 + H_2O$$

hints: Visualise heating a Group 2 nitrate, it gives a white solid residue, oxygen, and a coloured nitrogen dioxide gas.
walkthrough:
Spot the visible product**
Calcium nitrate decomposes on strong heating: $$2Ca(NO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2CaO + 4NO_2 + O_2$$ $CaO$ is white solid and $O_2$ is colourless, so the only thing you actually see is brown fumes of $NO_2$ evolving.
Final answer: brown fumes of $NO_2$ given off

hints: Let the oxidation state of N be x, use $O$ as -2 and the overall ion charge of -1 to solve for x.
walkthrough:
Calculate from charges**
In $NO_3^-$, each $O$ is $-2$. Let $N = x$: $$x + 3(-2) = -1$$ $$x = +5$$ So nitrogen is in oxidation state +5.
Final answer: +5 / V

hints: Check which element increases in oxidation state from left to right in equation 1, $Al$ to $[Al(OH)_4]^-$ versus $N$ in $NO_3^-$ to $NH_3$.
walkthrough:
Track oxidation numbers**
$Al$ starts as $0$ and ends up in $[Al(OH)_4]^-$ where $Al$ is $+3$, so its oxidation state rises, meaning loss of electrons. Nitrogen falls from $+5$ in $NO_3^-$ to $-3$ in $NH_3$. Therefore $Al$ is the species oxidised.
Final answer: aluminium / $Al$ is oxidised

hints: Focus on the lone pair on nitrogen in $NH_3$ and what a Bronsted-Lowry base does with $H^+$.
walkthrough:
Use the lone pair to accept $H^+$**
$NH_3$ has a lone pair on nitrogen. A Bronsted-Lowry base is an $H^+$ acceptor, so $NH_3$ uses that lone pair to accept $H^+$: $$NH_3 + H^+ \rightarrow NH_4^+$$ That is why ammonia is basic.
Final answer: $NH_3$ acts as an $H^+$ acceptor / proton acceptor using its lone pair.

hints: Count how many $OH^-$ groups are bonded to $Al$ and recall the shape for four bonding pairs with no lone pairs on the central atom.
walkthrough:
Count regions around $Al$**
In $[Al(OH)_4]^-$ the central $Al$ has four $Al-O$ bonding pairs and no lone pairs. Four pairs arrange to minimise repulsion in a tetrahedral shape with bond angles about $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Start from the $P^{2+}(g)$ ion and show removal of one electron to form $P^{3+}(g)$.
walkthrough:
Define third ionisation**
Third ionisation energy is the energy to remove the third electron, i.e. remove one electron from the gaseous $2+$ ion: $$P^{2+}(g) \rightarrow P^{3+}(g) + e^-$$ State symbols must be gas.

hints: Look at the 1st, 2nd and 7th to 10th points already plotted to see the overall direction of the values.
Think about where phosphorus has its outer electrons and after which removal you start breaking into an inner shell.
walkthrough:
Show a steady rise for 3rd to 5th**
Phosphorus is in Group 15 with 5 outer shell electrons. Removing 3rd, 4th and 5th electrons all come from the same n=3 shell with increasing positive charge pulling back, so plot three points rising gently above the 2nd value.

Make the big jump to the inner shell**
The 6th electron must come from the n=2 inner shell, much closer to the nucleus with less shielding. So the 6th point jumps much higher, and the increase from 5th to 6th is the largest step. The 7th point given is already very high, confirming this pattern.
Final answer: general increase from 3rd to 6th ionisation; largest jump shown is between 5th and 6th ionisation energies, plotted points rise steadily then jump sharply to 7th value.

hints: Use the fact that both elements are non-metals with no free electrons or ions to predict conductivity and bonding type.
Recall nitrogen is $N_2$ gas and white phosphorus is $P_4$ molecules, both held together by weak forces between discrete molecules.
walkthrough:
Nitrogen as simple covalent gas**
Nitrogen exists as discrete $N_2$ molecules with strong covalent bonds inside each molecule. There are no mobile electrons or ions, so conductivity is poor. Weak London forces between molecules give a simple molecular structure.

Phosphorus as simple covalent solid**
White phosphorus exists as discrete $P_4$ molecules, also covalently bonded within the molecule. Again no delocalised electrons, so conductivity is poor and the lattice is simple molecular, held by weak intermolecular forces.

Final answer: nitrogen: poor electrical conductivity; covalent bonding; simple structure
phosphorus: poor electrical conductivity; covalent bonding; simple structure

hints: Remember iodine crystals contain discrete $I_2$ molecules held by London forces, not ions or a giant network.
walkthrough:
Copy the iodine model**
Solid iodine is a simple molecular lattice of $I_2$ molecules. Solid nitrogen is the same, just $N_2$ molecules in place of $I_2$, held by weak London dispersion forces.
Final answer: simple molecular (lattice structure)

hints: Split the triple bond into its components, one bond formed by end-on overlap along the bond axis.
Consider how the remaining two bonds are formed by sideways overlap above and below the bond axis.
walkthrough:
Form the $\sigma$ framework**
Bring two P atoms together along the bond axis. One p orbital from each overlaps head-on, concentrating electron density directly between the nuclei. This is the single $\sigma$ bond.

Add the two $\pi$ bonds**
The two remaining pairs of p orbitals, perpendicular to the bond axis, overlap side-on above and below (and in front and behind) the axis. Each side-on overlap gives one $\pi$ bond, so together with the $\sigma$ bond you get $P\equiv P$.
Final answer: one $\sigma$ bond formed by head-on overlap of p orbitals; two $\pi$ bonds formed by side-on overlap of p orbitals.

hints: Compare the numbers 485 and 944 $kJ mol^{-1}$ and link larger bond energy to harder bond breaking and lower reactivity.
walkthrough:
Link bond strength to reactivity**
Breaking the triple bond is usually the key step in reaction. $P\equiv P$ needs only $485 \, kJ mol^{-1}$ while $N\equiv N$ needs $944 \, kJ mol^{-1}$, almost double. The weaker P-P triple bond breaks far more easily, so $P_2$ reacts much faster than very inert $N_2$.
Final answer: $P\equiv P$ is much weaker than $N\equiv N$ so $P_2$ is more reactive than $N_2$.
